title: Everyday Windows protection
summary: Use accounts, encryption, and permissions deliberately.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: A standard account reduces the impact of everyday mistakes and malicious programs by limiting administrative actions. Use an elevated context only when a task requires it. User Account Control provides an elevation boundary and a prompt for approval or credentials; approving an unfamiliar prompt without checking its origin defeats the intended protection. Local accounts and organization-managed identities have different administration paths, so verify which identity is actually being used.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: A firewall controls traffic according to rules, while antivirus tools look for malicious behavior or known threats. Disabling either control broadly to solve a connection problem creates unnecessary exposure; investigate the specific application and rule instead. BitLocker protects data on an encrypted volume, but access to a running, unlocked system still matters. Store recovery information through the approved process before making changes that could affect boot or encryption. For shared files, effective access depends on both share permissions and filesystem permissions, so test using the intended user account.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
